query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small, uniform amount of nickel (Ni) into the initial W–Cu composite will suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions, thereby improving the effective thermal conductivity of the joint.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite with discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments dispersed within a pure Cu matrix that, when untreated, shows phase separation and interfacial void formation under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 vol% Ni into the composite during powder processing before densification (e.g., via blending and subsequent spark plasma sintering) so that Ni is uniformly distributed at the W/Cu interfaces.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled sintering conditions (moderate temperatures that avoid excessive diffusion and allow proper wetting, and moderate pressure) with subsequent service in environments emulating the high heat-transfer and irradiation conditions typical of joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence of Ni is expected to promote the formation of a stabilized, Ni-rich interfacial layer between W and Cu, reducing interfacial energy and inhibiting the nucleation of voids and phase separation.
generation.mechanism: Ni acts as a sintering aid and interfacial wetting agent by increasing mutual solubility at the W–Cu boundaries. This minimizes the driving force for phase separation and void formation during both the thermal treatment and irradiation, thereby maintaining continuous, highly conductive interfaces that enhance overall thermal conduction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated composite, the Ni-modified composite will exhibit a significantly reduced density of interfacial voids and phase segregation, leading to higher measured thermal conductivity under the same thermal cycling and irradiation stresses.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composite is prone to developing interfacial voids and phase-separated regions during processing and under service conditions, which degrade the thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold within a processing window that avoids excessive diffusion (e.g., sintering temperatures optimized to allow Ni distribution without forming unwanted secondary phases) and under service conditions that mimic realistic thermal loads and irradiation levels; deviations from this window may reduce the effectiveness of the Ni-component.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ni concentration and processing parameters require further experimentation, and the long‐term stability of the Ni-enriched interface under extended irradiation remains to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: (1) a W–Cu composite with ~5 vol% Ni uniformly incorporated, and (2) a control composite without Ni. Process both under identical spark plasma sintering conditions. Subject the samples to accelerated thermal cycling and irradiation tests that simulate joint service conditions. Characterize interfacial structures and measure thermal conductivity before and after testing.
measurements: Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., laser flash analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-doped composite does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in interfacial void formation and phase separation, or fails to show improved thermal conductivity relative to the control after subjected to thermal cycling and irradiation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Hot Uniaxial Pressing and Pressureless Sintering of AlCrCuFeMnNi Complex Concentrated Alloy—A Comparative Study

Abstract: AbstractExternal pressure is often applied during sintering to obtain materials with improved properties. For complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), this processing step is commonly performed in vacuum. However, this can promote the evaporation of elements and increase the oxide content, thereby degrading the properties of the alloy. In this study, we compared the microstructures and properties of AlCrCuFeMnNi CCA samples obtained by hot uniaxial pressing sintering (HPS) and pressureless sintering (PLS) using a helium atmosphere purified by an oxygen getter system. The powders were prepared from mixtures of CrFeMn, AlNi and Cu and sintered by HPS at 900 °C for 1 h with an applied pressure of 30 MPa and by PLS at 1050 °C for 1 h. The samples were characterised using X-ray diffraction, scanning and transmission electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, electron backscattering diffraction, density measurements and hardness tests. Vacuum brazing of Al2O3 and 3D printed Ti6Al4V lap-joints using high entropy driven AlZnCuFeSi filler

Abstract: AbstractIn this work, we studied the brazing characteristics of Al2O3 and 3D printed Ti–6Al–4V alloys using a novel equiatomic AlZnCuFeSi high entropy alloy filler (HEAF). The HEAF was prepared by mechanical alloying of the constituent powder and spark plasma sintering (SPS) approach. The filler microstructure, wettability and melting point were investigated. The mechanical and joint strength properties were also evaluated. The results showed that the developed AlZnCuFeSi HEAF consists of a dual phase (Cu–Zn, face-centered cubic (FCC)) and Al–Fe–Si rich (base centered cubic, BCC) phases. The phase structure of the (Cu–Al + Ti–Fe–Si)/solid solution promises a robust joint between Al2O3 and Ti–6Al–4V. In addition, the joint interfacial reaction was found to be modulated by the brazing temperature and time because of the altered activity of Ti and Zn. The optimum shear strength reached 84 MPa when the joint was brazed at 1050 °C for 60 s.
